rows.reference: Vendidad (Videvdad), Fargard 4: the grades agerepta, avaoirishta and aredush, then graded penalties for blows and wounds (sections 26 to 33 in avesta.org's outline; section number of the definitions not confirmed)
rows.original: agərəpta, avaoirišta, arəduš (terms as recorded in the households annex, row ZO-3)
rows.translation: J. Darmesteter, SBE 4 (sacred-texts.com reproduces the 1880 text; avesta.org credits the 1898 American edition)
rows.says: Rising to strike a person, coming at them to strike, and striking them with evil intent are graded offences punished by lashes. Repeating them, or not atoning, makes the offender a peshotanu, liable to two hundred lashes with each of two whips. The law names no class of victim.
rows.bearing: K0 and K1: Clear teaching as a wider rule for traditionalists (rule 7), provisionally: it punishes malicious blows against any person and, with the death grade (next row, now verified), a blow that kills. Its reach to people outside the community is not stated, and Vendidad 7 (now verified) grades protection by faith in another setting. The lashes are court penalties (context, rule 5). Speaks for one branch only, so it cannot make K0 or K1 taught for the whole tradition.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (wider rule; traditionalists only; provisional as to reach)

rows.reference: Vendidad, Fargard 4, the grade after the bone-breaking grade: one who smites a man 'so that he gives up the ghost' (Darmesteter); section number not shown in the search record
rows.translation: J. Darmesteter, SBE 4: 1880 text on sacred-texts.com (ninety stripes with each whip); 1898 text on avesta.org (ninety with the Aspahe-astra, seventy with the Sraosho-charana)
rows.says: A man who smites another so that he gives up the ghost is punished with ninety stripes with the Aspahe-astra and ninety (avesta.org: seventy) with the Sraosho-karana. If he does not atone, he is a peshotanu, liable to two hundred with each. No class of victim is named. Darmesteter's introduction reads this grade as manslaying ('the manslayer gets off with ninety stripes'). Caution, kept from the previous verifier's recollection and not verified: some philologists take the Avestan verb to mean losing consciousness rather than dying.
rows.bearing: Clear teaching for traditionalists that killing a person by a malicious blow is a punished wrong (K1 and K0 as a wider rule; rule 7). The light penalty is graded protection, not permission (rule 2); the floggings are court penalties (context, rule 5). It does not say whether the death was intended; it reaches at least a death caused by a blow struck with evil intent. If the verb means loss of consciousness, it adds nothing beyond the row above. One branch only.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (traditionalists; on Darmesteter's reading of the verb as death)

rows.reference: Yasna 33.2 (Ahunavaiti Gatha)
rows.original: akəm drəgvāitē ... zastōibiiā (from memory; not checked against an edition)
rows.translation: L. H. Mills, SBE 31 (base; re-seen this pass); C. Bartholomae via Taraporewala; modern Zoroastrian renderings by D. J. Irani, F. Azargoshasb and the Zarathushtrian Assembly (A. A. Jafarey) differ (earlier records)
rows.says: Mills: whoever 'does evil to the wicked by word, or with thought (and plan), or with both the hands', or turns his dependant to the good, furthers the will of Ahura Mazda. Mills' note reads it as saying that harming the wicked by denunciation, scheming or physical force counts the same as guiding the good. Earlier records: Irani makes the object 'Evil'; Azargoshasb keeps fighting the wicked; the Assembly has 'foils the wrongful'.
rows.bearing: K1: commends deliberate physical harm by private persons to one class of people, the follower of the Lie (drəgvant), so it bears on K1's protection of 'the wicked'; not a court or war text (rule 5 does not exclude it). But it does not name killing, and translators divide on whether its object is people or evil, so on its own it is Implied as to killing (rule 4 by analogy). It supports the hard reading of Yasna 31.18 and is part of why K1 is Unclear. K0: no direct bearing; it names no gain, anger or revenge and frames the act as doing God's will (whether religious hostility counts as 'hatred' is a cross-tradition question). K3: none.

rows.reference: Yasna 31.18 (Ahunavaiti Gatha)
rows.original: sāzdūm ... snaiθišā (researchers' transcription; not checked against an edition)
rows.translation: L. H. Mills, SBE 31 (1887), sacred-texts.com (base; seen this pass); C. Bartholomae via I. J. S. Taraporewala (1951), avesta.org mirror (seen this pass); D. J. Irani and A. A. Jafarey (their wording not seen verbatim this pass); Weekly Zoroastrian Scripture Extract 255 (avesta.org)
rows.says: Mills: '(And you, ye assembled throngs!) let not a man of you lend a hearing to Mãthra, or to command of that sinner ... for home, village, region, and province he would deliver to ruin and death. But (fly ye to arms without hearing), and hew ye them all with the halberd!' The bracketed words are Mills' additions. Mills' heading says the speaker turns to the congregation, forbids them to listen to his opponents' doctrines, warns of the ruin and death that would follow, and appeals to the sword. Bartholomae: resist them with a weapon. The search record reports that Irani's and Jafarey's renderings also end in a call to fight; the earlier record has Irani's 'grip the sword'. WZSE 255 reads the weapon as purity and righteousness. The verb sāzdūm is rendered from 'resist' to 'cut down'.
rows.bearing: K1: Unclear (rule 6). It calls on the assembled hearers, not a ruler, to take up a weapon against a class of persons, so it bears directly on K1 and rule 5 does not exclude it. On one reading it is armed defence of the community against those who would bring house and village to ruin and death, which falls within K1's exception or is communal war (context b). On Mills' wording, where the danger comes from listening to the sinner's teaching and the hearers are to fly to arms 'without hearing', it comes close to a command to kill the followers of a false teacher, which K1 forbids. The verb, the weapon (literal or spiritual) and the target are disputed, so it is not the plain approval of a completed killing that rule 2 needs. K0: framed as defence, not gain, anger or revenge. K3: armed resistance; 'them all' refers to the followers of the false teacher and draws no line between fighters and others, but neither protects nor targets non-combatants as such.
rows.verification: VERIFIED (search): sacred-texts.com sbe31009.htm (Mills, Yasna XXXI) and zoroastrian.org.uk y28to34b.htm (Bartholomae), in search results this pass; earlier ZA-10, ZA-11 and Article I section G; seen: "hew ye them all with the halberd"; "for home, village, region, and province he would deliver to ruin and death"; Bartholomae: resist "with a weapon"
rows.check: searched and confirmed; corrected: Mills' wording, previously unconfirmed, is now seen and is the strongest rendering ('hew ye them all with the halberd', addressed to the assembled hearers); Irani's exact wording not re-seen

rows.reference: Vendidad 3.14 to 3.21, the man who carries a corpse alone (the execution near the end; section numbers not shown in the search record)
rows.translation: J. Darmesteter, SBE 4: 1880 text on sacred-texts.com; 1898 American edition on avesta.org
rows.says: A man who has carried a corpse alone is defiled and kept apart. When he reaches an advanced age class (Hana, Zaurura or Pairishta-khshudra), the worshippers of Mazda shall order a strong, vigorous and skilful man to flay him and cut off his head on a mountain top (1880 text); the 1898 text has the head cut off his neck in his enclosure on the mountain top, with 'to flay him alive and cut off his head' as an alternative in a note. The body is given to the vultures, with a formula declaring that the man has repented. Darmesteter's note: he is put to death by the law just before he would have died in the course of nature.
rows.bearing: A deliberate killing of a man attacking no one, for a ritual offence. It is ordered by 'the worshippers of Mazda' as a body and carried out by an appointed man, and Darmesteter's note and introduction treat it as a legal penalty, so it is read as context (a) (rule 5). K1 names religious leaders and crowds among those it binds, so the judicial reading rests on taking the community's order as a legal authority, which the traditionalists' own Denkard 5 and the Sad Dar's general rule (uncounted) support. No source was found treating it as a private killing. Fairness: other traditions' communal executions must be classed the same way.

rows.check: searched and confirmed (was UNVERIFIED); corrected: the two editions differ (the 1880 text adds flaying)

rows.reference: Vendidad 9.47 to 9.57 (section III, 'The false cleanser; his punishment'; section numbering differs between the two editions)
rows.translation: J. Darmesteter, SBE 4: 1880 text on sacred-texts.com; 1898 text on avesta.org
rows.says: The ungodly Ashemaogha 'cleanses the unclean without knowing the rites of cleansing according to the law of Mazda'. Penalty: he 'shall be taken to a desert place; there they shall nail him with four nails, they shall take off the skin from his body, and cut off his head'. In the 1880 text on sacred-texts.com this wording is in a note to the section; the 1898 text on avesta.org gives the penalty as a numbered section. Darmesteter's introduction: a repentant false cleanser is still flayed and beheaded, but his soul is saved.
rows.bearing: A deliberate killing of a non-attacker for a ritual offence, carried out by 'they' (the community) under religious law, which Darmesteter calls capital punishment expressly pronounced by the Vendidad. Context (a) on the judicial reading (rule 5), as with the corpse-carrier row. Unclear only if its judicial character were shown to be disputed within the tradition, which was not found. Whether the 1880 note reflects the Avestan text itself should be checked against an edition; the 1898 edition and the introduction place it in the text.

rows.says: A would-be healer must first prove himself with the knife on worshippers of the daevas, not of Mazda. If three daeva-worshippers die under his knife, he is unfit to practise for ever; if three cures succeed, he is fit for ever. If, unfit, he then treats a worshipper of Mazda and wounds him with the knife, he pays the penalty for wilful murder (baodho-varshta).

It leaves unresolved whether Fargard 4's assault law protects people outside the community, which is why the traditionalist result is provisional.

K1.label: Unclear (rule 6)
K1.reason: Deciding texts: Yasna 31.18 and 33.2 (Gathas, Tier 1, accepted by every branch), both re-seen by search in this pass. Yasna 31.18 in Mills is addressed to the assembled hearers, not a ruler. It says not to listen to the sinner's teaching or commands, because he would bring home, village, region and province to ruin and death, and ends 'hew ye them all with the halberd'. Bartholomae has 'resist ... with a weapon'. The reformist study series WZSE 255 reads the weapon as spiritual, and the verb sāzdūm is rendered anywhere from 'resist' to 'cut down'. So the verse bears directly on K1: it concerns private persons and a class of people, and rule 5 does not exclude it. But its reach is unresolved. On one reading it is armed defence of the community against those who bring ruin and death, which falls inside K1's exception or is communal war (context b). On Mills' wording, where the danger comes from listening to the teaching, it comes close to a command to kill the followers of a false teacher. The verb, the weapon and the target are disputed words, so this is a rule 6 case. It is not the plain approval of a completed killing of a non-attacker found in Numbers 35:26 to 27, Numbers 25 with Psalm 106:30 to 31, Abū Dāwūd 4361 or Seneca's De Ira 1.15.2. Yasna 33.2 (Mills: one who 'does evil to the wicked by word, or with thought ... or with both the hands' does Mazda's will) approves physical harm to the follower of the Lie by private persons but does not name killing. On its own it is Implied as to killing, but it supports the hard reading of 31.18. Yasna 47.4 and 46.6 (both now verified) set hostility, not killing, and are Implied. Support in texts every branch accepts is only Implied (30.6, 29.1, 49.4 and 32.11; 48.7 is unverified), so K1 is not taught for the whole tradition. Traditionalists also accept the Gathas, so the Unclear result applies to them too. Their Vendidad adds the following. Fargard 4 (the assault grades, and the death grade now verified) teaches K1 as a wider rule, provisionally, with a light penalty that is graded protection, not permission (rule 2). Vendidad 7 (now verified) names wilful murder as an offence but grades protection by faith in a case of unintended death (context f). The executions of Vendidad 3 and 9 (now verified) are ordered by the community and carried out by an appointed man ('put to death by the law' in Darmesteter's note), so they are context (a). Vendidad 8.31 to 32 (now verified) only declares a status (rule 4). The Vendidad 18.65 kill clause is still unverified and does not decide. Reported beside the label, not deciding: the Sad Dar 9 (outside the corpus, verified) forbids killing anyone without the authority of high priests and kings, except people caught in unnatural intercourse, whom anyone may kill; and the Zand on Vendidad 18 calls the courtesan with three men 'guilty of death'. Dependency: if the project reads 31.18 in Mills' wording as a command to kill the followers of a false teaching, K1 becomes Contradicted for every branch (rule 2). If it reads 31.18 as defence or communal war, and 33.2 as not reaching killing, the label becomes: not contradicted; taught in one branch only (traditionalists, provisionally); Implied only in the Gathas.

K0.label: Taught in one branch only (traditionalists, as a wider rule, provisionally); Implied only in the Gathas, which every branch accepts; not contradicted
K0.reason: No counted text permits killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. In the Gathas (every branch), fury against human life is the false gods' choice (30.6, re-seen in Bartholomae and Insler). Threatening life and seizing a household's inheritance mark the follower of the Lie (32.11, now verified). Those who spread violence and cruelty are condemned (49.4, 29.1). All of these are Implied, so K0 is not taught in texts every branch accepts. The content of 48.7's call to put down violence was seen but its verse number was not, and it would reach the anger clause only. Traditionalists: Fargard 4 punishes malicious blows against any person, including a blow that kills (the death grade, now verified), and Vendidad 7 (now verified) names wilful murder (baodho-varshta) as an offence. Together these are Clear teaching as a wider rule (rule 7), provisional because their reach to non-Mazdeans is not stated and Vendidad 7 grades protection by faith. Yasna 31.18 and 47.4 frame armed resistance and ill-will towards the follower of the Lie as defence and as service to God, not as gain, anger or revenge. If religious enmity is held to be 'hatred' under K0 (a decision to make once for all traditions), 31.18 would make K0 Unclear as it does K1. Yasht 9.18 (a royal revenge killing, unverified) is context (a) and (b). Under the branch rule, a result for traditionalists alone does not make K0 taught for the whole tradition.

K3.label: Silent

objections.label: K0
objections.objection: The label decides in advance a question that its own reason leaves open. The reason says Yasna 31.18 and 47.4 frame the action against the follower of the Lie 'not as gain, anger or revenge'. That list quietly leaves out hatred. The reason then concedes that if religious enmity counts as hatred, 31.18 makes K0 Unclear, which it calls 'a decision to make once for all traditions'. That decision has not been made. The K1 reason treats the defence frame of 31.18 as disputed, so the K0 reason cannot treat it as settled. The link to hatred is textual, not only a question of K0's wording. The same Gathas, verified by search, tell everyone to 'be ill unto the Liar' (47.4). They call a man who is very good to a Liar a Liar himself (46.6). They commend doing evil to the follower of the Lie 'with both the hands' (33.2, Mills). On the hard reading, the killing in 31.18 targets the very class the Gathas command hostility towards. Rule 6 gives Unclear when a counted text bears directly on the wording and its reach is unresolved. Other traditions facing the same kind of open point are labelled Unclear while it is pending. Stoicism's K0 asks whether drowning a newborn judged useless is 'for your own gain'. Islam's K0 asks whether killings for insult or apostasy are 'anger, hatred or revenge'. Christianity's K0 asks whether Phinehas's zeal is anger. Only Judaism's verifier took the line this label takes (religious grounds are not K0 motives). Judaism and Christianity already disagree on Phinehas, so the project has to choose one rule. Until it does, the neutral label is Unclear.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (reach unresolved). Rule 1: Yasna 31.18, 33.2, 46.6 and 47.4 are Tier 1, accepted by every branch and VERIFIED (search). Consistency with the K0 labels for Stoicism, Islam and Christianity.
objections.proposed: K0: Unclear (rule 6), all branches. It becomes 'not contradicted; taught in one branch only (traditionalists, provisionally); Implied only in the Gathas' if either of two things happens: (i) 31.18 is settled as defence, war or a spiritual weapon; or (ii) the project decides, for every tradition at once, that killing commanded against a religious or moral class to protect the community is not killing 'out of hatred'. It becomes Contradicted (all branches) only if 31.18 is settled as a command to kill people who are not attacking and that killing is held to be out of hatred. Rewrite the motive sentence so that it names all four motives and says which one is open.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: Rule 2 is misstated and the other traditions' results are misdescribed. The reason says 31.18 is 'not the plain approval of a completed killing that rule 2 needs'. It contrasts it with Numbers 35:26 to 27, Numbers 25 with Psalm 106, Abū Dāwūd 4361 and De Ira 1.15.2, presented as plain approvals. Both parts are wrong. Rule 2 is met by a text that 'permits, commands or approves'. A command needs no completed killing, so if 31.18 commands killing people who are not attacking, it contradicts K1 whether or not any killing follows. The project has also not labelled all those comparators as plain approvals. Christianity labels Numbers 35:26 to 27 Unclear (judicial or private character disputed), with Phinehas as a second hard case of the same kind. Judaism labels it only provisionally Contradicted. Islam's result on Abū Dāwūd 4361 waits on verification. The real reason 31.18 is Unclear is that its verb, its weapon and the object of 'them' are disputed words.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 2 (permits, commands or approves); rule 6 (a disputed word).
objections.proposed: Delete 'completed killing' and the claim that the listed texts are plain approvals. Say instead that De Ira 1.15.2 is Contradicted because its words are not disputed, while 31.18 turns on disputed words. It is Unclear by the same rule as Christianity's Numbers 35:26 to 27 and the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa, though by a different limb: disputed words, not a narrowing reading.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The hard reading leans on Mills' bracketed words and on a target the verse does not name. The row's bearing has the hearers flying to arms 'without hearing', and the label calls the addressees 'the assembled hearers'. Both phrases come from Mills' brackets ('(fly ye to arms without hearing)', '(And you, ye assembled throngs!)'), which the row itself marks as Mills' additions. The label also says 'them all' are 'the followers of a false teacher'. In Mills' wording as quoted, the only person named is 'that sinner', in the singular, and 'them all' has no plural personal antecedent. The row itself lists the target as disputed. The hard reading still stands without the brackets. The unbracketed 'let not a man of you lend a hearing ... hew ye them all with the halberd' addresses a plural audience of private persons and commands action against a group. So the label holds, but the reasons overstate the case.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 1 (only what the counted text says decides; a translator's bracketed addition is not the text); rule 6.
objections.proposed: Base the private-actor finding on the unbracketed plural 'a man of you'. State the hard reading as 'a command to cut down the sinner and those with him because of the danger of his teaching', not 'his followers'. Do not use 'without hearing' as evidence. Record the object of 'them' (persons, or the words and teachings themselves) as a disputed Textual part for the Register.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The strongest case that Unclear is too harsh: every rendering in the rows, Mills' included, gives the verse's own reason, that the sinner would deliver home, village, region and province to ruin and death. On the verse's own terms that is defence of others against deadly harm, or communal war. Only Mills says 'hew'; Bartholomae's 'resist ... with a weapon' names no killing. Hinduism's verifier read Atharvaveda 10.1, a lethal rite against sorcerers, 'on the hymn's own terms' as defence, and labelled K1 Taught. Read the same way, 31.18 would not make K1 Unclear. The case fails because the Hinduism verifier drew the line at an attack already under way, and said a rite against an enemy who is not attacking would be Unclear (rule 6). In 31.18 the danger lies in the future and comes through hearing a teaching: the first remedy the verse gives is not to listen. That is not plainly 'needed to stop them from killing or gravely harming someone'. War is not a clean way out either. If the opponents are dissenters inside the community rather than another people, the verse is a religious leader calling a crowd to arms, and K1 binds both. So Unclear stands. But the reason says the defence reading 'falls inside K1's exception' without saying what test it applied.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6; K1's exception; rule 5 (religious leaders and crowds are bound, and war is context only between communities); consistency with Hinduism's Atharvaveda 10.1 row.
objections.proposed: Keep Unclear. State the test openly: a lethal measure falls within the exception only if, on the text's own premise, the target is attacking or about to attack. A danger that comes through a teaching does not qualify. Apply the same test to Hinduism's Atharvaveda rites, so that the two traditions are judged by one line.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The strongest case that Unclear is too gentle: sources/translations.md makes Mills the project's base translation for the Gathas. On the project's own text, then, the verse tells private persons to 'hew ye them all with the halberd'. Rule 6 lets a narrowing reading count only if it comes from the tradition's counted texts, its classical commentators or an authorised body. For reformists there is none: WZSE 255 is a modern study series and counts only as evidence of dispute. The other Gathic verses push the same way rather than against it: 33.2 commends harm 'with both the hands', 47.4 says 'be ill unto the Liar', and 46.6 counts goodwill to a Liar as a mark of a Liar. The closest biblical parallel is Deuteronomy 13 (the enticer). Judaism and Christianity escaped a contradiction there only because the corpus itself gives that law a judicial frame (Deuteronomy 17; the Mishnah). 31.18 has no such frame in any text reformists accept. The case fails because rule 6 also accepts 'a disputed word' on its own. The verb (resist or cut down), the weapon (literal or spiritual) and the object of 'them' are disputed between the project's two philological renderings, not only by apologists. Insler and Humbach, the standard modern translations, have not been read (translations.md). So Unclear stands, but only on the disputed-word limb, which makes it fragile. The stated dependency is incomplete in two ways. First, the project cannot 'read 31.18 in Mills' wording' by choice: the dispute has to be settled textually, through Insler, Humbach, Kellens and Pirart, and the Zand on 31.18. Second, the result could split by branch. If the words are settled towards Mills, reformists have no narrowing reading and would be Contradicted. Traditionalists might stay Unclear through their own texts. One is Yasna 12.9: Peterson has the religion cause 'weapons to be set down', and the researchers' transcriptions, unchecked, show the same weapon word (snaiθiš), although the epithet's reading is disputed. Another is Denkard 3 and 5 (Tier 2, unverified), which confine lawful killing to sentence by religion and king, much as Aquinas and Augustine do for Christianity.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 6 (a disputed word; narrowing by counted texts or classical commentators); rule 2; branch rule (rule 1); METHOD.md section 9, decision 7; sources/translations.md (Mills is the base; Insler and Humbach unread).
objections.proposed: Keep Unclear (rule 6), all branches, and say that it rests on the disputed-word limb only. Restate the dependency as follows. If Insler, Humbach and the Zand settle 31.18 as a command to kill people who are not attacking, K1 is Contradicted for the reformist branch. It is Contradicted for traditionalists too, unless Yasna 12.9 or a verified Pahlavi reading narrows the verse, in which case it is Unclear for them. If the verse is settled as resistance to attackers, war or a spiritual weapon, K1 is not contradicted; taught in one branch only (traditionalists, provisionally); Implied only in the Gathas. Make Insler and Humbach on 31.18, and the Zand on it, the next research step.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: This objection also applies to K0. The traditionalist 'taught' rests on Darmesteter's renderings of two words and on a reach that has not been shown. (i) The K0 reason says Vendidad 7 'names wilful murder (baodho-varshta) as an offence'. That is Darmesteter's rendering. The row's own avesta.org gloss is 'done with full conscience', which reads as a general class of offence done knowingly, not murder; in 7.38 the penalty is for wounding with the knife. (ii) The death grade of Fargard 4 rests on 'gives up the ghost', and the row records an unverified philological view that the verb means losing consciousness. The assault law still forbids striking anyone with evil intent, and that reaches killing by blows, so the support survives, but on that wider ground only. (iii) Rule 7 and METHOD.md section 3 require the wider rule to reach everyone K1 protects. Fargard 4 says 'a man' and names no class. But Vendidad 7.36 to 40, in the same book, has trainee surgeons practise on daeva-worshippers, treats three of their deaths only as a bar to practice, and gives the full penalty for wounding a Mazda-worshipper. That makes the reach of 'a man' a real question, not a formality. (iv) The K1 reason calls Fargard 4's light penalty 'graded protection'. In rule 2 that term marks a lesser penalty for some victims than for others. Ninety lashes applies to every victim, so it is simply a light penalty, which rule 2 says is not permission.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 and METHOD.md section 3 (a wider rule must reach everyone); rule 2 (graded protection); strength ratings (Clear teaching must be unmistakable).
objections.proposed: Traditionalist sub-result: 'taught in one branch only, provisionally: Clear teaching as a wider rule through the assault law of Fargard 4. Its reach to non-Mazdeans is unresolved (Vendidad 7.36 to 40), and the death grade and baodho-varshta depend on Darmesteter's renderings.' Describe Vendidad 7 as setting 'a penalty for an offence done knowingly (baodho-varshta; Darmesteter: wilful murder)'. For Fargard 4, replace 'graded protection' with 'a light penalty is not permission (rule 2)'. Keep 'graded protection' for Vendidad 7's difference by faith.

objections.label: K1
objections.objection: The dependency names only 31.18. For traditionalists, two unverified items could change the branch result even if 31.18 is settled in the benign direction. (i) The Vendidad 18.65 kill clause. If it is verified and read of a human woman, as the Zand note on the same passage reads it, it is a counted text that names no court and no actor. That gives Unclear for traditionalists at least (rule 5, last sentence; rule 6), or 'contradicted in one branch' (rule 3) if read as a private licence. (ii) Darmesteter's 'first comer' note. If it is traced to the Zand, it is a classical reading that anyone may kill an offender guilty of a margarzān ('worthy of death') crime. That would make the judicial character of the Vendidad's capital penalties disputed within the tradition, so rule 5's last sentence would give Unclear for traditionalists. Also, the context (a) reading of Vendidad 3 and 9 rests mainly on uncounted texts (Darmesteter, the Sad Dar, the unverified Denkard 5). In Vendidad 9 the executioners are an unnamed 'they', not an appointed man. Treating them as context (a) is still consistent with how Judaism and Christianity treat Deuteronomy 21:18 to 21, a community execution under law, so the classification can stand.
objections.proposed: Add both items to the K1 dependency for the traditionalist branch. Say that Vendidad 3 and 9 are context (a) because the law itself prescribes the penalty, with the uncounted texts in support only.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The strongest case that Silent is too gentle: if 31.18 is read as communal war, Mills' 'hew ye them all' orders a whole hostile group cut down with no line between fighters and others. That resembles Deuteronomy 20:16 ('nothing that breathes'), which made K3 Contradicted for Judaism and Christianity. The case fails. Deuteronomy 20:16 names everyone alive, children included by its own words. 31.18 names only 'them', a group the verse presents as bringing ruin and death, and says nothing about people who are not fighting. It is Implied at most, and Silent stands. But the reason asserts as fact that 'them all' means 'the followers of the false teacher', which the quoted words do not show (see the K1 objection on Mills' brackets). Yasna 53.9's 'Lord righteous who will smite them from life' may be God rather than a ruler; if so it is a petition (rule 4), not court context. The search is also thin: the Yashts are unverified and no Pahlavi text on the conduct of war was searched.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 8 (Silent); rule 4 (petitions and divine acts); rule 2 as applied to Deuteronomy 20:16 elsewhere.
objections.proposed: K3: Silent in counted texts (provisional), in the same form as Hinduism's label. Describe 'them all' as a disputed group, Implied at most. File 53.9 as a petition or as ruler context; neither decides.

K1.label: Unclear (rule 6), all branches
K1.reason: Deciding text: Yasna 31.18 (Gathas, Tier 1, every branch). It is VERIFIED (search) in Mills, the project's base translation, and in Bartholomae. The verse tells a plural audience of private persons not to listen to the sinner's words, because he would deliver home, village, region and province to ruin and death. It then tells them to take a weapon against 'them'. It bears directly on K1, and rule 5 does not exclude it: no court or ruler is named, and if the opponents are inside the community, it is a religious leader calling a crowd, and K1 binds both. Three of its words are disputed (rule 6): the verb (Mills 'hew', Bartholomae 'resist'); the weapon (literal, or spiritual as in WZSE 255, which shows the dispute but cannot narrow the verse); and the object of 'them' (persons, and if so which, or the teachings). On one reading it is armed resistance to people who threaten death, which falls within K1's exception or is war (context b). On another it is a command to cut down a group because of the danger of their teaching, which K1 forbids; rule 2 needs only a command, not a completed killing. The danger lies in the future and comes through hearing, so the defence reading is not plain. Yasna 33.2 (harm to the follower of the Lie 'with both the hands'), 47.4 and 46.6 set hostility, not killing. They are Implied as to killing; they support the hard reading but cannot decide it. The Unclear result rests on the disputed-word limb alone: for reformists, no counted text, classical commentator or authorised body narrows the verse. Support in texts every branch accepts is only Implied (30.6, 29.1, 49.4 and 32.11; 48.7 is unverified). Traditionalists share the Unclear result. Their Vendidad adds a wider rule, Fargard 4's assault law with its death grade, at Clear teaching. That support is provisional, because its reach to non-Mazdeans is unresolved (Vendidad 7.36 to 40) and two of its words rest on Darmesteter's renderings. The executions in Vendidad 3 and 9 are context (a), because the law itself prescribes them. Vendidad 8.31 to 32 only declares a status (rule 4). The 18.65 kill clause and Darmesteter's 'first comer' note are unverified; the Pahlavi books and the Sad Dar are not counted. Dependency: if Insler, Humbach and the Zand settle 31.18 as a command to kill people who are not attacking, the label is Contradicted for the reformist branch, and for traditionalists too unless Yasna 12.9 or a verified Pahlavi reading narrows the verse (then Unclear for them). If they settle it as resistance to attackers, war or a spiritual weapon, the label is: not contradicted; taught in one branch only (traditionalists, provisionally); Implied only in the Gathas. That alternative is subject to the unverified traditionalist items above.

K0.label: Unclear (rule 6), all branches
K0.reason: No counted text approves killing for gain, anger or revenge. The open point is hatred. On the hard reading of Yasna 31.18 (see K1), the Gathas command armed action against the follower of the Lie. That is the same class towards whom 47.4 (verified) says to 'be ill', to whom 46.6 forbids goodwill, and whom 33.2 commends harming by hand. Whether a killing commanded against that class, to protect the community, is a killing 'out of hatred' is unresolved, and so is the K1 dispute over 31.18 itself. Rule 6 gives Unclear. Stoicism (the 'gain' question), Islam (killings as religious penalties) and Christianity (Phinehas's zeal) are labelled the same way while the same kind of question is pending. If the hard reading of 31.18 fails, or if the project decides once for all traditions that such killing is not 'hatred', the label becomes: not contradicted; taught in one branch only; Implied only in the Gathas. The traditionalist support is provisional. It rests on Fargard 4's assault law against malicious blows and on Vendidad 7's penalty for an offence done knowingly (baodho-varshta, which Darmesteter renders 'wilful murder'), and its reach to non-Mazdeans is unresolved. The Gathic support is 30.6, 32.11, 49.4 and 29.1; 48.7 is unverified. The uncounted Pahlavi texts (Denkard 3: killing from passion is unlawful) agree but cannot decide. Yasht 9.18 (unverified) is a king's revenge in war, context (a) and (b).

K3.label: Silent in counted texts (provisional)
K3.reason: No verified counted text protects or targets people who are not fighting. Yasna 31.18 (Mills: 'hew ye them all with the halberd') and 53.8 to 9 concern force against a group presented as bringing ruin and death, and against raiders and persecutors. 'Them all' is a disputed group and draws no line between fighters and others, so it is Implied at most. It is unlike Deuteronomy 20:16, which names everything that breathes. 53.9's 'Lord righteous' may be God (a petition, rule 4) or a ruler (context). Yasna 12.2 to 3 renounces raiding the community's own settlements (Implied, and in part only). The Yashts on victory and Yasht 9.18 are unverified, and no Pahlavi text on the conduct of war was searched, so the silence rests on a thin search.

challenge.consistency_notes: Compared with the listed hard cases. (1) Stoicism, De Ira 1.15.2: Contradicted, because a household killing of newborns is approved in words nobody disputes. Yasna 31.18 differs only because its verb, weapon and object are disputed. That is a rule 6 limb, not the 'completed killing' distinction the proposed reason drew, since rule 2 also covers commands. (2) Judaism and Christianity, Numbers 35:26 to 27 and Phinehas: Judaism has them provisionally Contradicted and Christianity Unclear (judicial or private character disputed). The Zoroastrian reason should not describe them as settled plain approvals. 31.18 is Unclear by a different limb, disputed words rather than a disputed setting. (3) Deuteronomy 13, the enticer, is the closest parallel to the hard reading. Judaism and Christianity treat it as court context, at most Unclear, because the corpus itself (Deuteronomy 17; the Mishnah) gives it a judicial frame. 31.18 has no such frame in any text reformists accept, so its Unclear rests only on the disputed words and is more fragile. Traditionalists may have a narrowing in Yasna 12.9 and the Denkard, which plays the role that Aquinas and Augustine play for Christianity. (4) Sunni Islam, Abū Dāwūd 4361: Contradicted in one branch once verified, because a private killing is declared unpunished. Islam's verifier made K0 Unclear for killings presented as religious penalties, and I apply the same approach to Zoroastrian K0. (5) Mahāyāna, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra: Unclear because the same counted sūtra narrows its own hard passages. 31.18 is Unclear without any such internal narrowing. (6) Hinduism, Atharvaveda 10.1: read as defence because, in the hymn's own world, the attack is already under way; rites against enemies who are not attacking would be Unclear. I apply the same line to 31.18: its danger lies in the future and comes through hearing a teaching, so the defence reading is not plain. Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12 (unverified) names hatred, which is why Hinduism's K0 is the most exposed there. The Zoroastrian hatred question comes instead through the Gathas' command to be 'ill' towards the follower of the Lie. (7) Article I's households annex made Zoroastrian 'no cruelty' Unclear on Yasna 33.2 alone, because that wording forbids injury. Here 33.2 is Implied as to killing because K1 forbids only killing, which is consistent. (8) Open project-wide choice: Judaism's verifier holds that religious grounds are not K0 motives, while Christianity, Islam and Stoicism label the equivalent open point Unclear. Judaism and Christianity disagree even on the same text (Phinehas). The project lead should settle once whether religiously commanded killing counts as 'hatred' (or 'anger') under K0, and then relabel all affected traditions together. Until then, the consistent label is Unclear.
